name: Recovering deleted D drive data
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person experienced a severe data loss incident caused by a Claude Code (referred to as "CC") session that ran a PowerShell command gone wrong. When asked to create a OneDrive sync relationship for D:\transfer, CC executed a `-Recurse -Force` deletion of the existing D:\transfer directory contents, replaced it with an empty folder, and linked that to OneDrive — permanently destroying everything that had been in D:\transfer. CC then compounded the damage by attempting its own recovery, which likely wrote to D: and further reduced recovery odds.

Claude walked through every available recovery path in priority order: OneDrive Recycle Bin, Windows Recycle Bin, checking the local OneDrive sync folder, Previous Versions/VSS shadow copies, File History, and raw sector recovery tools. The person confirmed the drive is an SSD, which activates TRIM and dramatically compresses the recovery window. Claude recommended Recuva over TestDisk for this specific situation, explaining that TestDisk addresses partition-level problems while Recuva targets deleted files on an intact file system — which is the correct tool for a `-Recurse -Force` deletion scenario. Claude also provided the `fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify` command to check whether TRIM was active before the person had to leave.

The person was physically away from the machine (approximately 11 miles) for a minimum of two hours, retrieving personal belongings from another location. The computer was left running and idle, which Claude noted was the best possible state for it. The person expressed significant distress and a sense of resignation about the loss. Claude acknowledged that CC bore responsibility for the catastrophic command execution and should never have used `-Force` on a populated directory without explicit confirmation from the user.

chat_messages.text:
Let me make sure I understand the situation precisely before walking you through recovery options.

You ran a PowerShell command (or had one run for you) that was intended to mark an existing folder as OneDrive-synced, but instead it created a new empty folder with the same name — effectively replacing/destroying the contents of your D: drive folder. The data was deleted from PowerShell, not through the Recycle Bin.

Here's every recovery avenue, ordered from highest to lowest probability of success:

---

## 1. OneDrive Recycle Bin (Check First — Fastest Win)

If the folder was previously synced to OneDrive at all, deleted files often land in the **OneDrive cloud Recycle Bin**, not just the local one.

Go to onedrive.live.com → Recycle Bin (left sidebar). Files stay there **30 days** for personal, **93 days** for business/Microsoft 365.

---

## 2. Windows Recycle Bin

PowerShell's `Remove-Item` **without** the `-Force` flag sometimes sends files to the Recycle Bin. Check it immediately before doing anything else that writes to disk.

---

## 3. File History / Windows Backup

If File History was enabled on your machine:

**Settings → System → Storage → Advanced storage settings → Backup options** (or search "Restore your files with File History"). If it was backing up your D: drive, you can restore previous versions directly.

---

## 4. Previous Versions (Shadow Copies / VSS)

Right-click the folder location on D: → **Properties → Previous Versions tab**. Windows sometimes creates shadow copies automatically via System Restore or VSS. This is completely separate from File History and works even if you never manually set up backups.

---

## 5. OneDrive Version History

If any of those files *were* in OneDrive previously, every file has version history. Go to OneDrive online → find any surviving file → right-click → **Version history**. You can restore older versions individually.

---

## 6. Raw File Recovery Software (Undelete)

This works because when files are deleted, Windows only removes the directory entry — the actual data blocks stay on disk until overwritten. **Stop writing to the D: drive immediately** to maximize recovery odds.

Best tools:

- **Recuva** (free, by Piriform) — easiest UI, good for most cases
- **TestDisk / PhotoRec** (free, open source) — deeper scan, recovers without filenames
- **R-Studio** — paid, best recovery rate for complex situations
- **Disk Drill** — paid, good UI, solid results

Run any of these and recover **to a different drive**, never back to D:.

---

## 7. Check the OneDrive Sync Folder Itself

When OneDrive "made the folder available," it may have moved files into the OneDrive local sync directory rather than deleting them. Check:

`C:\Users\[YourName]\OneDrive\` and look for the folder name there. Files may be sitting there intact.

---

## 8. OneDrive "Personal Vault" or Selective Sync

Sometimes OneDrive moves files to online-only status rather than deleting them. In the OneDrive taskbar icon → check if files show as **cloud icons** (online-only) rather than being gone. You can force-download them.

---

## Priority Order Right Now

1. **Stop writing to D: drive** immediately
2. Check OneDrive Recycle Bin online
3. Check Windows Recycle Bin
4. Check `C:\Users\[You]\OneDrive\` for the folder
5. Check Previous Versions on the D: folder
6. Run Recuva on D: drive, recover to another drive

What was the PowerShell command that was run? That'll help me tell you exactly what happened and which of these is most likely to work.

chat_messages.text:
Oh hell. That's a junction/symlink operation gone catastrophically wrong — it didn't just delete a folder, it **force-deleted the contents of your existing D:\transfer to replace it with an empty directory**, then linked that empty directory to OneDrive. That's a `-Force` flag on a `New-Item` or `Remove-Item` that had no business being there.

Let's get your data back. Here's what actually happened and every recovery path:

---

## What CC Actually Did

Most likely command sequence:
```powershell
Remove-Item "D:\transfer" -Recurse -Force  # <-- this is what killed everything
New-Item -ItemType Junction "D:\transfer" -Target "$env:USERPROFILE\OneDrive\transfer"
```
Or a `mklink /J` with a pre-wipe step. The `-Recurse -Force` is the murder weapon.

---

## Recovery Paths, Best First

### 1. OneDrive Recycle Bin (Check RIGHT NOW)
go to **onedrive.live.com → Recycle Bin**. If D:\transfer was previously synced even partially, files may be there. 93 days for Microsoft 365, 30 days personal.

### 2. Windows Recycle Bin
Open it before doing anything. `-Force` usually bypasses it, but check anyway. Takes 10 seconds.

### 3. Check OneDrive Local Folder
```powershell
dir "$env:USERPROFILE\OneDrive\transfer"
```
Sometimes the operation moved rather than deleted. Slim hope but free to check.

### 4. Previous Versions / Shadow Copies
Right-click **D:\transfer** → Properties → **Previous Versions tab**. VSS snapshots are completely automatic on many Windows 11 systems and have nothing to do with OneDrive or File History.

### 5. File History
Settings → search "Restore your files with File History" — if it was running and covering D:, you're golden.

---

### 6. Raw Sector Recovery — DO THIS NOW IF ABOVE FAIL

**Stop writing anything to D: drive immediately.** Every byte written reduces recovery odds.

Get **Recuva** (free):
- recuva.com — download and install to C: or another drive
- Point it at D:\transfer
- Run deep scan
- Recover everything **to a completely different drive** (not D:)

If Recuva finds nothing or partial results, escalate to **R-Studio** or **Runtime GetDataBack** — paid but they reach sectors Recuva misses.

---

## One Critical Question

Was D:\transfer on an **SSD or HDD**?

If SSD — TRIM may have already zeroed those sectors, which compresses your recovery window to potentially **minutes** after deletion. If you're on SSD, stop everything and run Recuva right now before reading the rest of this.

If HDD — you have more time, data blocks persist until overwritten.

---

What do you want to tackle first? And do you know if D: is SSD or HDD?

content.text: Tell me why should I use this recovery instead of this thing called test disk?

chat_messages.text:
TestDisk and Recuva do different things.

**Recuva** recovers deleted files by scanning for orphaned file records and raw data signatures. It's what you want when a `-Recurse -Force` wipe is the cause — because the partition and file system are still intact, just the files are gone.

**TestDisk** recovers lost **partitions** and repairs **boot sectors**. It's the right tool when a drive won't mount, a partition disappeared, or the file system itself is corrupt.

Your D: drive is still visible and mountable — CC deleted the files, not the partition. That means **Recuva is the correct tool for your specific situation.** TestDisk would find nothing useful here because there's nothing wrong with the partition structure.

Run Recuva first. If for some reason D: itself becomes inaccessible when you get back, then TestDisk becomes relevant. But right now Recuva is the right call.
